topic: Compile-Time Polymorphism with `constexpr` and Template Metaprogramming
explanation: This expert-level C++ concept explores compile-time polymorphism achieved through `constexpr` functions and template metaprogramming.  It delves into how the compiler generates highly optimized code by evaluating function calls and template instantiations at compile time, eliminating runtime overhead.  We'll examine the memory layout implications, focusing on how the compiler avoids runtime function calls and memory allocations by generating specialized code for different template arguments.  We'll also touch on the potential for increased compile times and code size when dealing with complex metaprograms.
code_example: std::cout << "2 to the power of 10: " << twoToTen << std::endl;
example_explanation: The compiler evaluates `factorial(5)` and `powerOfTwo<10>()` at compile time.  No runtime function calls are generated for these calculations. The compiler substitutes the results (120 and 1024 respectively) directly into the `main` function. This eliminates the runtime overhead of function calls. The assembly code will show direct assignment of the computed values to variables, without any call instructions to the factorial or powerOfTwo functions.  The memory layout is optimized as no stack space is allocated for function calls.  However, complex template metaprogramming can lead to increased compile times due to the compiler generating numerous specialized template instances.  Additionally, extensive use might result in larger binary sizes because the compiler includes the specialized code for all used template instantiations.
